items.title: Pak-US reset?
items.description: SINCE early 2025, Pakistan’s relations with the US have taken an upturn after years of mutual disenchantment. Why did the US opt for this reset? And will this bonhomie last? Historically, Pakistan and the US have come close only when their interests converged. America has preferred a transactional relationship with Pakistan based on specific issues of its geopolitical agenda. The recent thaw in ties can, therefore, be better understood in terms of how global geopolitics is evolving. It is no longer a unipolar world led by the US. Since the dawn of this century, several centres of power have arisen while the US remains entangled in long, distant wars. The US reliance on its military might to subdue adversaries has taken a heavy toll on America’s world standing. Into this evolving geometry of global power politics stepped Donald Trump, who has ruptured the trans-Atlantic alliance, pulled back support for Ukraine in its war against Russia, and sought to stabilise America’s ties with China. However, nothing has compromised America’s domestic and international standing more than the recent US-Iran war. As for Pakistan-US ties, three developments seem to have contributed to the recent thaw. First is Pakistan’s role in countering terrorism. In March 2025, President Trump thanked Pakistan in his State of the Union address to Congress for apprehending the mastermind of a bombing in Kabul on the eve of the US exit from Afghanistan. Later, Centcom chief Gen Michael Kurilla described Pakistan to Congress as a “ phenomenal partner in the world of counterterrorism ”. In June 2025, Trump hosted Pakistan’s army chief for lunch at the White House. And in August, BLA was designated as a terrorist organisation by the US. Three developments seem to have contributed to the recent thaw. Second, the US, like the rest of the world, saw Pakistan robustly counter Indian aggression in May 2025 . The US mediated a ceasefire on May 10. Pakistan acknowledged America’s positive role. New Delhi, on the other hand, was reluctant to acknowledge Trump’s role, even though India itself had asked the US to secure a ceasefire. Third, Pakistan’s mediatory role in the recent US-Iran conflict has convinced Washington of Pakistan’s important role as a net stability provider in the region. Meanwhile, America’s distrust of India has deepened because the latter has bought Russian oil while ignoring US sanctions, and has maintained continued economic ties with China while pretending to be a US partner to counterbalance China. America is no longer convinced that India can be a trustworthy counterweight to China. How will this reset impact Pakistan’s other key relationship? Islamabad’s close ties with Beijing are not unknown to Washington. The Chinese leadership is also well aware of the strategic nature of Sino-Pak relations. In an era where cooperation and confrontation coexist, Pakistan has ample space to pursue mutually beneficial relations with both China and the US based on its own national interest. India is upset at the uptick in Pakistan’s ties with the US, and its own failure to isolate Pakistan diplomatically. As for Afghanistan, the US has not shown any interest in it, even as the country is on the cusp of becoming a safe haven for world terrorists. The US is also aware of the fine balance that Pakistan has always maintained in its ties with both Iran and Saudi Arabia. How should Pakistan use this reset in its relationship with the US, even if it was transactional, for mutual benefit? Several promising areas can be identified: Pakistan must ensure that its share of flourishing trade with the US is maintained and enhanced. The US offers bright prospects for Pakistan’s yo­­ung, tech-savvy entrepreneurs, IT exports, startups, software de­­velopment, growing digital adoption, and e-commerce. American companies shou­­ld be encouraged to invest in Pak­istan’s shale oil potential and minerals sector , especially lithium, rare earth elements, and copper — crucial for the semiconductor industry, defence technology and robotics, among others. Other promising areas of cooperation include defence, security, and counterterrorism. Agriculture has been a legacy area of cooperation since the 1950s, as have education and public health. However, all this will only be possible if Pakistan addresses its policy and regulatory hurdles, cost of doing business, security risks, and infrastructure issues. Today’s Pakistan stands tall as a competent, self-confident power that can contribute to regional peace, stability, and development. However, this window of opportunity may be limited because global geopolitics is constantly evolving. What matters most is making the best use of the recent thaw in Pakistan-US ties while preserving our other key relationships, including with China. The writer is a former ambassador to the US and is currently serving as chairman of the Sanober Institute. Published in Dawn, October 25th, 2026

items.title: Tomato prices remain high as pepper gets cheaper in Lagos
items.description: The drop in pepper prices has brought some relief to traders and buyers in Lagos markets, but the high cost of tomatoes continues to weigh on traders’ sales and consumers’ purchasing power. Traders and consumers who spoke with the News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) in separate interview in Lagos described how changing prices had affected sales, household spending and the quantities of produce they could afford. They cited seasonal availability and transportation costs among the factors influencing the market. Malam Mohammed, a tomato seller at Costain Bus Stop, said he sourced his produce from Mile 12 Market, where prices varied according to variety, size and place of origin. He said a paint of tomatoes, which sold for N6,000 in August and September, now cost N7,000, while a basket had risen from between N35,000 and N40,000 to between N45,000 and N65,000. Mohammed explained that the high cost of tomatoes made it difficult for traders to maximise profits, adding that some customers complained about the sizes and quantities they received for the prices paid. “This business is not a straight business,” he said. He said the complaints had caused him to lose some customers, prompting him to reduce the quantity of tomatoes he purchased at a time to avoid losses from spoilage. Mohammed also said a large bag of pepper currently sold for between N30,000 and N40,000, although he could not recall its exact price in August and September because of fluctuations. Mrs Rukayat Sherif, another trader at Costain Bus Stop, said she bought tomatoes and pepper from Mile 12 Market because she trusted the source. She said a basket of Ghana tomatoes currently sold for between N40,000 and N45,000, compared with N50,000 and above in August and September. Sherif added that a paint of tomatoes now cost N7,000, against between N4,000 and N5,000 in September. She said a small bag of pepper, which sold for between N30,000 and N35,000 in August and September, now cost between N20,000 and N25,000. Sherif noted that five pieces of tomatoes sold for N500, while pepper was also available for N500 in small rubber plates containing a generous quantity. She attributed the price changes partly to seasonal availability and transportation costs, explaining that some tomatoes damaged during transportation the previous week had been sold at reduced prices to prevent further deterioration. She expressed hope that tomato prices would fall to more affordable levels, adding that lower prices would improve sales and reduce customers’ complaints. Mrs Regina Owho, a tomato seller at Suru Market, Suru-Alaba, said large baskets of tomatoes currently sold for about N50,000, while smaller baskets cost between N35,000 and N45,000. Owho recalled that a basket sold for about N40,000 in August and September, although prices fluctuated during that period. She said the frequent changes made it difficult for traders to predict their purchasing costs, adding that the basket she bought on the day of the interview cost N40,000. Mrs Mary Chigozie, a resident of Vaughan Street, Costain, said she spent between N2,000 and N5,000 daily on tomatoes and pepper but had reduced the quantities used in cooking because of the high cost of tomatoes. She said small quantities of tomatoes that previously sold for N200 or N300 now cost N500 or N1,000. Chigozie explained that she sometimes combined pepper with tomato paste or prepared red-oil stew when fresh tomatoes became too expensive. She expressed concern that prices could rise further during the December festive period and urged the government to support and protect farmers. On pepper, Mrs Rukayat Rasheeb, a trader at Olaogun Street, Abule-Nla Junction, Costain, said a bag currently sold for between N45,000 and N60,000, the same price range recorded in August and September. She, however, observed that pepper was now more plentiful than during the earlier period. Rasheeb explained that prices generally declined when pepper was in season and increased when it became scarce. She expressed optimism that prices could fall further, while noting that transportation and loading expenses added to traders’ costs. Mr Okoro Ebubechi, who also sells pepper at Olaogun Street, Abule-Nla Junction, said he currently bought a small basket for N20,000, compared with between N30,000 and N40,000 in September. He attributed the reduction to increased availability during the current season, adding that transportation expenses influenced the prices charged by traders. Ebubechi said customers were buying larger quantities because pepper had become more affordable. He added that he sold pepper in different quantities, including portions worth N500, to accommodate buyers with varying budgets. He expected prices to rise again in December if pepper became less available. Mrs Odunayo Igwe, a pepper trader at Ilogbo Mosque, Apapa Road, said a bag currently sold for N30,000, the same price recorded in September. She explained that although the price had remained unchanged, pepper was now more plentiful than in September, when supplies were lower. Igwe also identified transportation costs as a factor affecting selling prices and expressed hope that prices would decline further. Mrs Patience Niju, a pepper seller at Suru Market, Suru-Alaba, said she currently bought a small bag for N25,000 and a larger bag for N40,000. She added that a small bag of shombo cost N20,000, while a larger one sold for N30,000. Niju said the prices were unchanged from August and September, but the bags contained more pepper in October. She welcomed the increased quantity, saying it encouraged customers to buy more and helped her sales move faster. Mrs Teni David, a civil servant residing in Iyana Ipaja, said N200 to N500 could now buy more pepper than in August and September, when the same quantity cost between N1,000 and N1,500. She said the increased availability had enabled her to buy larger quantities for household consumption. David attributed the seasonal glut partly to limited preservation facilities, explaining that large quantities of pepper entered the market as the produce ripened, prompting traders to sell quickly before it lost its freshness. She called on the government to establish more processing centres where farmers and traders could preserve and package pepper during periods of abundance. According to her, such facilities would help reduce waste and maintain supplies during the off-season. David warned that prices could rise again when the current season ended. Ms Mary Udonwa, another pepper consumer, said the produce had become more affordable, allowing households to buy larger quantities. She said she currently spent between N500 and N1,500 on pepper, depending on her needs. Udonwa explained that high prices in August and September had forced her to reduce the amount used in cooking, sometimes relying on small quantities or ground pepper when fresh pepper became expensive. She attributed the current reduction to increased market supply and suggested that some sellers might be lowering prices to avoid losses from spoilage. Udonwa also expected pepper prices to rise during the Christmas and New Year festivities. The post Tomato prices remain high as pepper gets cheaper in Lagos appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: NDLEA recovers tons of illicit drug consignments in nine states
items.description: The National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) has recovered tons of illicit drugs in Kano, Lagos, Bauchi, Niger, Edo, Ondo, Taraba, Oyo and Delta states. The Director, Media and Advocacy, NDLEA, Mr Femi Babafemi, said this in a statement on Sunday in Abuja. Giving a breakdown, Babafemi said a suspect was arrested in Warri, Delta with a huge cache of pharmaceutical opioids. These included 29,350 capsules of tramadol, 6,620 tablets of tramadol 200mg, 4,116 bottles of codeine syrup, 11,340 tablets of Rohypnol and 3,500 tablets of diazepam. “Others are 300 ampoules of pentazocine injection, 200 ampoules of diazepam injection, and quantities of tramadol 225mg, Molly and Cocodamol. “He was transferred along with a white Hummer bus from the Nigeria Police Force, Delta State,” he said. In a separate arrest at Enhere Junction, Warri, a 46-year-old physically challenged woman was arrested by NDLEA operatives on Oct. 19 with 6.0kg of skunk. Meanwhile, a 41-year-old suspect was also arrested on Oct. 19 in Adamasingba, Ibadan, Oyo State, following his initial escape from arrest when NDLEA officers seized 197.8kg of cannabis sativa from his house on Sept. 16. Babafemi said a raid in Gerawa area of Kano on Oct. 22 led to the arrest of a suspect and seizure of 159 blocks of cannabis sativa weighing 97.2kg. Also, NDLEA officers at the Lankaviri checkpoint, Yorro Local Government Area, Taraba, on Oct. 23, arrested another suspect with 95 blocks of compressed cannabis weighing 60.175kg. “The same day, the Nigeria Police Force handed over a suspect arrested at Dakka village, Bali LGA, with 112 blocks of compressed cannabis weighing 81.49kg,” he said. Similarly, in Niger State, another suspect was arrested by NDLEA operatives on Oct. 19 on Sabo-Kainji road, Borgu LGA, with 64,000 pills of opioids, including tramadol and diazepam. Babafemi said NDLEA officers also arrested another suspect on Oct. 21 at Nasaru Town, Ningi LGA, Bauchi State, where they seized 379kg of cannabis sativa packed in seven jumbo sacks. “Acting on intelligence, NDLEA officers on Oct. 20 raided a farm at Board-Ala, Akure South, Ondo, and recovered 56 bags of abandoned cannabis sativa weighing 583kg. “Two cannabis farms in Ugbada Forest, Uzebba, Owan West LGA, Edo, with an estimated yield of 2,023.14kg, were destroyed on Oct. 18 by NDLEA operatives. “They also burnt 450kg of processed cannabis at the site and took 97kg as exhibit,” he said. In a related operation at Ewe community, Owan West, another suspect was arrested with 35kg of the same psychoactive substance. With the same vigour, commands and formations of the agency across the country continued their War Against Drug Abuse (WADA) sensitisation activities to schools, worship centres, workplaces and communities, among others, in the past week. These include WADA enlightenment lectures to students and staff of Oje Grammar School, Ibadan, Oyo State; Government Day Secondary School, Kwamba, Niger State, Baptist Primary School, Olorunda, Ogun. Others are Government Secondary School, Yalea, Kano State; Community Secondary School, Igogoro, Enugu State; Urban Girls Secondary School, Onitsha, Anambra; and Kelebe Community Grammar School, Osogbo, Osun, among others. Babafemi quoted the NDLEA Chairman, retired Brig.-Gen. Buba Marwa, as commending the officers and men of Kano, Lagos, Bauchi, Niger, Edo, Ondo, Taraba, Oyo and Delta commands for their vigilance. This, he said, included their diligence, professionalism and intelligence-driven approach to the various successful operations. Marwa urged them and their colleagues across the country to sustain the tempo of the war against drug trafficking and substance abuse. The post NDLEA recovers tons of illicit drug consignments in nine states appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: IGP Disu proposes 200% gratuity, pension for retired officers
items.description: The Inspector-General of Police (I-G), Mr Olatunji Disu, has proposed a 200 per cent gratuity and pension for retired police officers as part of the ongoing reforms in the Nigeria Police Force. Disu told newsmen on Sunday in Abuja that the proposal was before a Presidential Committee, set up to examine police concerns and recommend sustainable solutions. He said the proposal was to intensify efforts to secure improved retirement benefits for personnel of the Nigeria Police Force (NPF) and address the longstanding pension challenges. The I-G also said that the committee was made up of representatives of the Ministry of Finance and the Office of the Accountant-General of the Federation. According to him, other representative in the committee are the National Salaries, Incomes and Wages Commission, the Budget Office of the Federation and the National Pension Commission (PenCom). “Under the proposed arrangement, eligible officers can retire on pension benefits linked to their last salaries, alongside the enhanced gratuity.” Disu said the package was also, expected to address recurring protests by serving officers, seeking to exit the Contributory Pension Scheme (CPS), a contentious issue within the force. “The initiative is aimed at resolving the outstanding pension liabilities, provide more adequate retirement benefits and create a more efficient pension administration system. “It also seeks to cover officers who retired before the new framework takes effect, with provisions to review their benefits in line with the revised terms, rather than limiting reform to future retirees,” he said. I-G said the intervention of President Bola Tinubu in the police pension crisis had raised expectations among retired officers, who had long complained about inadequate benefits, delayed payments and administrative bottlenecks. According to him, for many pensioners, timely access to benefits is essential for meeting household expenses and medical bills amid rising living costs. He said the Federal Government had cleared the backlog of pension payments that previously left some retirees waiting for up to two years and introduced pension increment. Disu revealed that some of the beneficiaries currently receive almost double of their previous payments. “Our engagement with the presidency, PenCom and other relevant institutions is seen as important to sustain the NPF reform momentum. “The committee is expected to recommend measures on outstanding liabilities, funding arrangements and benefit administration. “It is also, to provide a framework to resolve pension challenges and improve coordination among the institutions responsible for policy, funding and administration,” he said. He added that the proposal remained subject to the committee’s deliberations, relevant government approvals, funding arrangements and implementation guidelines. He said the 200 per cent gratuity should not be regarded as approved or existing entitlement, adding that the final outcome would determine whether it would be adopted. The post IGP Disu proposes 200% gratuity, pension for retired officers appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.description: Le développement du football national, la détection des talents nationaux et la valorisation des richesses culturelles sont au cœur de la Ligue de la souveraineté, une initiative présidentielle présentée le samedi 24 octobre 2026, dans la salle de conférence de Ouaga 2000, par le Camarade Adama GUIRA, responsable exécutif du projet. La cérémonie de présentation a connu la présence de la Camarade Annick PIKBOUGOUM/ZINGUÉ OUATTARA, ministre des Sports, de la Jeunesse et de l’Emploi, de l’ensemble des gouverneurs de région ainsi que des directeurs régionaux en charge du sport. Prévue de janvier à juin 2027 et exclusivement réservée aux Burkinabè, cette compétition ambitionne de renforcer les bases du football national en offrant aux joueurs issus des différentes régions un cadre d’expression, de progression et de visibilité. Elle vise à élargir le champ de détection des talents, à favoriser leur accès aux opportunités de progression sportive et à faciliter l’identification de joueurs susceptibles d’intégrer les différentes catégories de sélection nationale. Au-delà de la compétition, la Ligue de la souveraineté entend contribuer à l’émergence d’un football davantage structuré autour des ressources humaines et des potentialités locales. Les résultats attendus portent notamment sur une meilleure identification des talents dans les régions, le renforcement de la dynamique du football à la base et une plus grande visibilité des joueurs évoluant en dehors des principaux pôles sportifs. Cette approche vise à rapprocher les opportunités sportives des jeunes et à favoriser une valorisation plus large du potentiel footballistique burkinabè. L’autonomisation des bénéficiaires constitue également un enjeu important de cette initiative. En donnant aux joueurs un cadre de compétition et de valorisation de leurs compétences, le projet entend contribuer à leur épanouissement et élargir leurs perspectives d’évolution dans le domaine sportif. Les acteurs mobilisés dans le cadre de la Ligue de la souveraineté percevront un salaire et seront tous déclarés à la caisse, afin de leur garantir une meilleure protection sociale et de renforcer leur autonomisation. L’ambition est de faire du football un moyen de développement personnel et professionnel, tout en favorisant la reconnaissance des compétences acquises sur les terrains. Une attention particulière est également accordée aux anciens footballeurs vivant en région. Forts de leur expérience et de leur connaissance du milieu sportif, ces acteurs peuvent contribuer à l’encadrement des jeunes, à la transmission des savoir-faire et à la consolidation des dynamiques footballistiques locales. La Ligue de la souveraineté ouvre ainsi des perspectives de valorisation de leur expérience et de reconversion dans des domaines tels que l’encadrement, la formation et l’accompagnement sportif. L’enjeu est de mieux mobiliser ce capital humain au service de la relève et du développement durable du football national. La compétition porte par ailleurs une dimension culturelle et territoriale. En réunissant les régions autour d’un rendez-vous sportif commun, elle entend contribuer à la valorisation des identités locales, des traditions et du patrimoine culturel burkinabè. La mise en lumière de cette diversité doit favoriser les échanges entre les populations, renforcer le sentiment d’appartenance nationale et faire du sport un vecteur de cohésion sociale. Sur le plan organisationnel, la compétition se déroulera en deux poules, A et B. À l’issue de cette phase, les quatre premières équipes de chaque poule accéderont aux play-offs, réunissant huit équipes dans la phase décisive de la compétition. À travers la Ligue de la souveraineté, les résultats recherchés dépassent le cadre des performances sportives. Il s’agit de renforcer la détection des talents dans les régions, d’accroître les possibilités de progression des joueurs, de valoriser l’expérience des anciens footballeurs, de soutenir l’inclusion de la jeunesse et de mettre en lumière les richesses culturelles des territoires. En associant ces différentes dimensions, cette initiative présidentielle ambitionne de faire du football endogène un levier de développement sportif et de valorisation du potentiel humain national. De janvier à juin 2027, la Ligue de la souveraineté entend ainsi contribuer à une meilleure structuration du football à la base, à la promotion des talents burkinabè et au renforcement des dynamiques sportives régionales, dans une perspective de cohésion nationale et d’opportunités pour les bénéficiaires. DCRP/MSJE

items.title: NCCIA busts child pornography network, finds father involved in selling explicit videos of his children
items.description: ISLAMABAD: The National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA) has busted an international child pornography network in which a father was found involved in making and selling explicit videos of his own children, the agency said on Sunday. Islamabad NCCIA Additional Director Mohammad Shoaib Khan, speaking at a press conference in the capital, claimed this was the first case in Pakistan’s history where a father was found involved in such a heinous crime against his own minor children. “The accused was involved in making indecent videos of his children, aged between four and five, and selling them. The videos were bought and sold in secret Telegram groups through cryptocurrency,” he said. Khan added the investigation also revealed disturbing scenes of animal abuse in the videos. He said the ringleader of the gang belonged to Skardu and was arrested with the assistance of international agencies. During the investigation, important links and evidence were recovered from Islamabad, Multan and South Punjab, and raids were being conducted to arrest other network facilitators, according to Khan. “Those involved in such heinous crimes will be brought to justice,” he said. In another similar case, Khan said the agency arrested four members of a child pornography gang after investigating around 60 videos recovered from a child’s mobile phone. He said the suspect used to befriend children aged between six and 14 on Instagram, lure them with money and make indecent videos, which were then sold internationally via WhatsApp groups. Khan said two Chinese nationals had also been convicted earlier in this crime. Sharing details of another case, the additional director said a minor girl from Karachi attempted suicide after being fed up with harassment. The girl is currently under treatment at a hospital. Khan said the NCCIA team, with the help of the victim’s family, traced and arrested the main suspect from Islamabad in just 13 hours. He added that the suspect had been continuously harassing and blackmailing the victim for the last two to three years. “Providing justice to the affected families is our top priority. Strict implementation of a zero-tolerance policy against those harassing women and children is being ensured,” he said. The additional director further advised social media users to remain vigilant. “Think before uploading any indecent material. The law is in action; those uploading wrong content will not escape the law in any case,” he said. He urged citizens not to share their one-time password, bank account details or personal information with anyone and to beware of fake numbers on fake websites, as calling them may lead to emptying of accounts. “If you are a victim of cybercrime, do not remain silent; NCCIA stands with you,” he said, adding that citizens can call helpline 1799 for complaints, which is available 24 hours. ‘Zero-tolerance’ policy against cyber harassment of women, children According to a separate statement issued by the NCCIA, the agency’s Director General (DG) Syed Ali Nasir Rizvi directed adopting a zero-tolerance policy against “elements harassing citizens,” particularly women and children, on social media. The directions were made in a meeting attended by Khan, Director IT Atif Abbas, in-charge of social media Tayyaba Daulat, Public Relations Officer Mehboob Elahi, among others. The meeting, per the statement, was given a detailed briefing on social media monitoring, prevention of fake news, cyber harassment cases, public awareness campaign and digital handling of cybercrime complaints. “DG NCCIA issued directions to make citizens’ protection on social media, prompt redressal of complaints and institutional coordination more effective and active,” it said. The DG further ordered strict monitoring of accounts spreading fake news, negative propaganda against state institutions and fear and panic among the public, and indiscriminate action against those responsible, according to the statement. On October 23, NCCIA Karachi Zone claimed to have arrested suspects from three firms allegedly involved in production, promotion, and online sale of sexually explicit animated cartoons, animated child sexual abuse material, pornographic digital content and other digital designing services to international customers. A recent Unicef report revealed that an estimated 1.5 million children in Pakistan experienced online sexual abuse in one year. As per the report, around 85 per cent of perpetrators were known to the victims, aged between 12 and 17. Furthermore, 71pc of victims did not tell anyone, according to the Unicef report, while no child surveyed reported the abuse through formal channels — including police, helplines or social workers. Meanwhile, child protection NGO Sahil estimates that at least 1,914 cases of child abuse were reported across the country in the first six months of 2026. From January to June 2026, as many as 1,015 cases of child sexual abuse, 558 cases of abduction, 101 cases of missing children and 35 cases of child marriage were reported. Further, 98 cases of pornography following sexual abuse were also recorded. The Sahil report was compiled on the basis of data collected from different national and regional newspapers of all four provinces, including Islamabad Capital Territory, Azad Jammu and Kashmir and Gilgit-Baltistan. Of the total reported cases, 58 per cent of victims were girls. The data also showed that children aged 11-15 years were the most vulnerable to abuse.

items.title: BPP, ICPC rank among Tinubu govt’s best-performing agencies – Report
items.description: The Bureau of Public Procurement (BPP) and the Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission (ICPC) have emerged among the best-performing agencies under President Bola Tinubu’s administration in an independent service delivery assessment conducted by a coalition of civil society organisations. The assessment, highlighted at a roundtable in Lagos, recognised the two institutions for their contributions to transparency, accountability, protection of public resources and efforts to strengthen safeguards against corruption. The engagement brought together civil society leaders to examine the performance of selected ministries, departments and agencies (MDAs), with particular attention to institutional efficiency, public accountability and the delivery of measurable results. The BPP, led by its Director-General, Dr Adebowale Adedokun, received particular recognition for procurement reforms that reportedly saved the Federal Government approximately N1.1 trillion in 2025. According to the assessment, the savings demonstrate the potential of effective procurement regulation to reduce waste, curb inflated contract costs and ensure more responsible use of public funds. The Bureau has introduced measures to strengthen price intelligence and cost benchmarking, enabling government agencies to assess contract estimates against prevailing market prices and improve value for money in public spending. Other initiatives highlighted include the digitalisation of procurement processes, revised Standard Bidding Documents, updated procurement guidelines and the development of electronic procurement systems designed to improve efficiency and reduce opportunities for manipulation. The BPP has also pursued a National Debarment Policy to strengthen accountability for contractors involved in serious misconduct, alongside professional training and certification programmes for procurement officers. The coalition noted that effective procurement oversight could help reduce corruption risks, promote competition, improve investor confidence and ensure that public expenditure translates into better infrastructure and essential services. The ICPC was similarly recognised for its role in investigating corruption, enforcing relevant laws and promoting preventive measures to strengthen integrity within public institutions. The commission’s responsibilities include addressing abuse of office, protecting public resources and promoting ethical standards across government agencies. The assessment highlighted the importance of the ICPC’s work in public procurement, where inadequate oversight and corrupt practices can expose government finances to substantial losses. It also stressed the need for sustained anti-corruption efforts, professional investigations, credible enforcement and stronger collaboration among regulatory agencies, law enforcement institutions and civil society organisations. Beyond the performance of the two agencies, the Lagos roundtable examined the broader responsibility of government institutions to demonstrate measurable improvements in public service delivery. Participants argued that agencies should be assessed not merely on policies announced or activities undertaken, but on their tangible impact on citizens and the efficient use of public resources. They emphasised that institutions responsible for infrastructure, economic regulation, social services, public administration and national security must demonstrate transparency, efficiency and responsiveness to public needs. The coalition also called for continuous independent monitoring of government agencies, stressing that performance assessments should serve as an ongoing mechanism for identifying successful practices, exposing institutional weaknesses and encouraging reforms. For the BPP, sustaining the reported procurement savings will require stronger enforcement of regulations, improved project monitoring, wider adoption of digital systems and continued professional development. The assessment also underscored the importance of ensuring that lower contract costs translate into quality projects and tangible benefits for Nigerians. For the ICPC, participants stressed that sustained preventive measures, credible enforcement and institutional cooperation would remain essential to strengthening public confidence in the fight against corruption. The coalition maintained that recognising progress must go hand in hand with continued scrutiny to ensure that government institutions remain accountable and focused on delivering results. It said sustained engagement between civil society and public institutions would be critical to protecting public resources, improving governance and ensuring that government policies produce meaningful outcomes for Nigerians. The post BPP, ICPC rank among Tinubu govt’s best-performing agencies – Report appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: La rançon de la visibilité (par Arame NDIAYE)
items.description: Un live, une créatrice de contenus qui discute avec sa communauté sur TikTok. La scène est d’une banalité déconcertante. Mais il a suffi de quelques minutes pour que Rama, plus connue sous le pseudonyme de Miss Gorée , fonde en larmes en plein direct, la semaine dernière. À bout, l’influenceuse n’arrive plus à contenir ses larmes face à des personnes qui n’hésitent pas à la harceler jusque dans ses propres lives. Une situation loin d’être anodine pour cette guide touristique connue pour partager des informations sur l’île mémoire. En effet, lors d’un récent entretien accordé à Soleil Digital , la jeune femme pointait du doigt le comportement de certains hommes qui l’appellent uniquement pour lui faire des propositions indécentes. Mais il faut croire que c’est une fâcheuse habitude. Miss Gorée dénonce ainsi des agissements qui dépassent largement le cadre des réseaux sociaux. Car derrière les écrans, certains se permettent des actes qu’ils n’oseraient peut-être jamais assumer en face de leurs victimes. Voir aussi: [Vidéo] Rama, alias Miss Gorée : la créatrice de contenus qui fait découvrir l’île mémoire Le cas de Miss Gorée est loin d’être isolé. Sur TikTok, Facebook ou Instagram, les créatrices de contenus sont nombreuses à subir des insultes, des remarques déplacées et des attaques sur leur physique. La créatrice de contenus Anitah Bamba, elle aussi, fait partie de ces femmes dont l’apparence devient un sujet de discussion pour des internautes qui semblent oublier qu’un écran ne donne pas tous les droits. Trop grosse, trop maigre, trop ceci ou pas assez cela : les commentaires fusent, souvent sous couvert d’humour. Le bodyshaming est devenu une pratique banalisée, au point que certains ne voient même plus le mal qu’ils font. Le parcours de Halima Gadji rappelle également que la célébrité ne protège pas des blessures. L’actrice, connue pour son rôle de Marème dans la série « Maîtresse d’un homme marié », avait elle-même parlé des difficultés personnelles et des attaques auxquelles elle était confrontée. Son décès, en janvier 2026, a relancé les discussions sur la pression qui accompagne la notoriété et sur les conséquences des violences en ligne. Sans réduire son histoire à ces seules attaques, il est nécessaire de rappeler que les personnalités publiques restent des êtres humains, avec leurs fragilités et leurs combats. Au Sénégal, les réseaux sociaux sont devenus un espace où chacun peut donner son avis sur tout. On peut ne pas apprécier une créatrice de contenus, ne pas aimer ses vidéos ou désapprouver ses prises de position sans l’insulter, la rabaisser ou lui faire des propositions indécentes. La liberté d’expression ne devrait pas servir de prétexte à toutes les dérives. D’ailleurs, la loi sénégalaise prévoit des sanctions pour certains abus commis en ligne. Les injures, la diffamation, les menaces ou encore la diffusion non autorisée de contenus privés peuvent, selon les circonstances, donner lieu à des poursuites. La loi n° 2008-11 du 25 janvier 2008 sur la cybercriminalité et les dispositions du Code pénal encadrent notamment ces infractions. Internet n’est donc pas une zone de non-droit, même si certains semblent encore l’ignorer. Miss Gorée partage des informations sur Gorée, fait découvrir son île et échange avec sa communauté. Elle ne devrait pas avoir à subir des humiliations pour exercer cette activité. Pas plus qu’Anitah Bamba ne devrait avoir à justifier son physique, ni qu’une autre créatrice de contenus devrait accepter les insultes au nom de sa visibilité. Arame NDIAYE

items.title: The nuclear danger at sea
items.description: Dawn’s October 23 editorial rightly warned about India’s nuclear-armed submarine patrols. The danger is larger than a new vessel at sea. It is a sea-based nuclear force growing alongside precision-strike capabilities, missile defence and a false confidence in initiating military action. Imagining that these developments confer a first-strike advantage or create a safe space for war is imprudent. Pakistan has the capability and resolve to preserve the strategic balance. Retired Lt-Gen Mazhar Jamil, Adviser to the National Command Authority, warned at the International Institute for Strategic Studies on October 13 that continuous at-sea deterrence further weakens the credibility of India’s declared no-first-use policy and points towards an offensive strike posture. He added that unannounced submarine-launched ballistic-missile tests, with operationalised weapons aboard submarines, raise the risks of misperception and escalation. Pakistan reserves the right to take all appropriate measures to protect its security and the regional balance. At the Islamabad Non-Proliferation Conference a week later, retired Lt-Gen Khalid Kidwai, also an adviser to the National Command Authority, reinforced the warning, saying Pakistan would review its options if India sought to impose a strategic imbalance. In June 2026, the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (Sipri) estimated that India had a stockpile of 190 nuclear warheads and 12 of these deployed on a nuclear-powered ballistic-missile submarine for occasional deterrence patrols. That estimate is too low and arrives seven years late. Prime Minister Modi announced the INS Arihant’s first deterrence patrol in 2018 and the Indian Navy again patrolled it again during the 2019 crisis . India has three operational ballistic-missile submarines (SBBN), with a fourth expected in 2027. Next year, the four SSBNs will have a combined capacity to launch missiles carrying up to 72 warheads from 24 tubes. A larger fleet of 12 nuclear ballistic and attack submarines is envisaged in the 2030s . Aggressive posturing India’s professed no-first-use pledge cannot be judged without taking into account its capabilities and political conduct. A ready, concealed launch platform gains a different meaning when combined with counterforce ambitions, missile defence and talk of pre-emption. General Kidwai’s assessment about a possible strike at ‘zero notice’ should be read in that setting. Pakistan has never allowed its deterrence capability to be neutralised by India’s posture that is taken as routine modernisation. Strategic stability rests on a credible balance and Pakistan will maintain it under all circumstances. General Zubair Hayat, former Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Committee, argued at the Islamabad Non-proliferation Conference that the old international order is giving way without an equitable replacement. His strategic point applies here: strategic exemptions for a favoured state, followed by alarm at its neighbour’s balancing measures, do not produce equal security. The nuclearisation of the Indian Ocean did not begin when Pakistan raised its concerns. It began with India’s risky choices, enabled and fuelled by an international tendency to treat its ambitions as benign. May 2025 demonstrated the danger of that assumption on land and in the air. On the first anniversary of Marka-i-Haq, President Asif Ali Zardari reiterated that India used Pahalgam’s false flag as a guise for premeditated strikes. India ignored Pakistan’s offer of a neutral investigation and had to endure a defeat and loss of face. Pakistan’s calibrated conventional response, under political authority, restored conventional deterrence, while Full Spectrum Deterrence preserved the strategic ceiling. The Indian Air Force grounded itself, and the Indian Navy’s carrier strike group cut a hasty retreat to safety. The ceasefire followed Islamabad’s response and New Delhi’s call for third-party mediation. There was no safe band of war then, and there is none at sea now. A lesson for India Retired Lt-Gen Sarfraz Sattar, who served as Director General of the Strategic Plans Division, has also warned that emerging technologies and great-power competition threaten nuclear stability. The March 2022 BrahMos launch into Pakistan showed why. A supersonic nuclear-capable missile crossed the border in peacetime; India waited nearly two days before acknowledging it and did not accept Pakistan’s call for a joint inquiry and preserved the risk of escalation. Three years on, India carried that risk into wartime by employing BrahMos against another nuclear power — the first such instance . The sea-leg of India’s nuclear triad and dual-capable missiles are sinews of a Hindutva-inflected policy of hegemony and coercion. Pakistan’s declared Full Spectrum Deterrence covers the range of threats it faces, and it clearly signals that aggression at any level or in any domain risks a response that will deny objectives and impose costs; an adversary cannot dictate the level at which a confrontation will remain. Political authority, prepared forces and credible options give that warning its weight. As India’s posture changes, Pakistan will take the measures necessary to safeguard its sovereignty and strategic balance. Risk reduction has value, but it cannot substitute for deterrence or responsible political choices. Dialogue is worthwhile when it reduces the incentives and opportunities for unilateral force, not when it is offered as a substitute for Pakistan’s defence. Pakistan always stands ready to impose greater costs for on any misadventure that India may undertake, including the maritime domain. In May 2025, Islamabad demonstrated that its calibrated notch-up response should not be read to mean that every aggression will meet the same ceiling. General Kidwai also recommended adding a “ plus ” to Pakistan’s quid-pro-quo plus response strategy. The lesson for India is direct. Neither an expanding submarine fleet nor other developments give it an edge over Pakistan’s response to aggression. Pakistan has demonstrated both resolve and the means to defend itself. It will preserve the balance on which peace depends. In the Subcontinent, the true enemy is the delusion that war can be kept safely on a lower rung. That Indian aspiration makes the unthinkable look controllable. It’s an illusion that a war can be started low, kept low, and stopped on command. A political choice driven by Hindutva and Akhand Bharat may begin the escalation; interaction decides where it goes. Field Marshal Asim Munir expressed the governing reality most aptly: there is no space for war in a nuclearised environment.

items.title: Understanding Your Milk Options: A Dietitian’s Guide to Choosing the Right Milk
items.description: By Tito Ipinmoye Buying milk used to be simple. You walked into a supermarket, reached for a familiar tin or sachet, and carried on with the rest of your shopping. Today, that same trip can leave many people standing in the dairy aisle far longer than they expected. I remember shopping at one of the large supermarkets when I noticed a young couple standing in front of the milk shelf. They had been there for what felt like ten minutes, carefully picking up one product after another, turning the packs over to read the labels before placing them back. The wife was scrolling through Instagram, almost desperately, as though she hoped someone had recently posted the answer to the question they were trying to solve. “Which milk should we buy?” I couldn’t help but overhear parts of their conversation. Interestingly, they weren’t comparing brands or prices. They were trying to understand the different options available. Should they choose dairy milk or a non-dairy alternative? And if dairy was the right choice, what exactly was the difference between Full Cream Milk and Filled Milk? They wanted to make the right choice but weren’t sure what those terms meant. Eventually, I smiled and walked over. “Hello,” I said. “I’m sorry to interrupt. I’m a dietitian, and from what I’ve overheard, I think I can help explain the differences.” Within a few minutes, what had seemed like a complicated shopping decision suddenly became much clearer. They thanked me, picked the product that best suited what they were looking for and continued with the rest of their shopping. That encounter reminded me of something I have observed repeatedly throughout my years of practice: many consumers assume that milk is simply… milk. Yet today’s supermarket shelves tell a very different story. Before deciding which milk to buy, many consumers are first faced with an important question: Should I choose dairy milk or a non-dairy alternative? For those who choose dairy milk, there is another decision to make. Understanding the difference between Full Cream Milk, Filled Milk and age-appropriate milk products is key to choosing the option that best meets their needs. The challenge is that these differences aren’t always obvious to the average shopper. As a result, many people make their decisions based on familiarity, price or attractive packaging rather than understanding what the product was designed to do. Making informed food choices doesn’t always begin with eating something different. Sometimes, it begins with simply understanding what you’re buying. And that’s exactly where we’ll begin. Understanding the Two Main Milk Options When we think about the milk aisle, it can sometimes feel as though there are endless options. The first decision is much simpler than many people realise. Broadly speaking, there is Dairy milk and non-dairy milk Dairy milk comes from animals, most commonly cows, although goat’s and sheep’s milk are also consumed in many parts of the world. It naturally provides high-quality protein, calcium and several essential vitamins and minerals that support growth, bone health and overall wellbeing. For consumers who choose dairy milk, there is one more decision to make. Not all dairy milk products are the same. Within the dairy category, the two most common options consumers will come across are Full Cream Milk and Filled Milk . While both are dairy products and both provide important nutrients, they differ in their fat composition and are designed to meet different nutritional needs and consumer preferences. Understanding these differences is the next step in choosing the milk that’s right for you. Understanding Your Options Standing in that supermarket, I realised the couple weren’t just trying to choose a brand. They were trying to understand which type of dairy milk best suited their needs. Once you’ve decided that dairy milk is the right choice for you, the next step is understanding the different dairy products available. Peak’s dairy range, for example, includes Full Cream Milk, Filled Milk and Peak 456 Growing-Up Milk . Although they all contain dairy ingredients, each has been developed to meet different nutritional needs and life stages. Rather than thinking of these as different versions of the same product, it helps to think of each one as serving a different purpose. Peak Full Cream Milk is designed to provide complete dairy nutrition for everyday family use. Peak Filled Milk, on the other hand, offers consumers another dairy option with a different fat composition while still providing important nutrients such as protein and calcium. Peak 456 Growing-Up Milk is specially formulated to support the nutritional needs of children aged four to six years. Understanding what each product is designed to do makes choosing the right one much easier. Let’s take a closer look at each one. Peak Full Cream Milk When most people think of milk, Full Cream Milk is usually what comes to mind. Made from whole cow’s milk, it naturally contains milk fat, giving it the rich, creamy taste many people enjoy. It also provides complete dairy nutrition by supplying high-quality protein, calcium and a range of essential vitamins and minerals that contribute to bone health, muscle function and overall wellbeing. One example within this category is Peak Full Cream Milk, which is available in both powdered and evaporated formats. Its versatility makes it suitable for drinking, breakfast cereals, smoothies, tea, coffee, cooking and baking, making it a practical choice for everyday family use. Best suited for: Families looking for complete dairy nutrition for everyday use. Peak Filled Milk Filled Milk is a dairy milk product in which part or all the natural milk fat has been replaced with vegetable oils. While this gives it a different fat composition from Full Cream Milk, it continues to provide important nutrients such as high-quality protein, calcium and essential vitamins. Peak Filled Milk offers consumers another dairy milk option that combines these nutritional benefits with a different fat composition to suit varying dietary preferences. Rather than thinking of Filled Milk as “better” or “worse” than Full Cream Milk , it is more helpful to understand that each product has been developed to meet different consumer needs. The right choice depends on your nutritional requirements, health goals and personal preferences. Best suited for: Consumers looking for a dairy milk option with a different fat composition. Peak 456 Growing-Up Milk Children have different nutritional needs at different stages of growth, which is why age-appropriate milk products have an important role in supporting a balanced diet. Peak 456 Growing-Up Milk is specially formulated for children aged four to six years. In addition to providing high-quality protein and calcium, it is fortified with essential vitamins and DHA, an omega-3 fatty acid that supports normal brain development during childhood. By providing nutrients tailored to this stage of growth, Peak 456 helps support the nutritional needs of young children as part of a healthy, balanced diet. Best suited for: Children aged 4–6 years. A Simple Guide to Choosing the Right Milk Choosing the right milk doesn’t have to be complicated. Once you understand what each product is designed to do, the decision becomes much simpler. If you’re looking for… A suitable option is… Complete dairy nutrition for the family Peak Full Cream Milk A dairy milk option with a different fat composition Peak Filled Milk Nutrition designed for children aged 4–6 years Peak 456 Growing-Up Milk Before adding any dairy milk product to your shopping basket, ask yourself three simple questions: Which dairy milk do I need? Full Cream or Filled milk Who am I buying this product for? Does this product meet my nutritional needs and suit how I intend to use it? Answering these questions can help you move beyond attractive packaging or familiarity and choose the product that best suits your needs and those of your family. Choosing with Confidence Standing in that supermarket, I realised the young couple weren’t looking for the “best” milk. They were looking for clarity. Like many consumers, they simply wanted to understand the options available, and which one best suited their needs. Their questions weren’t unusual. They reflected the uncertainty many shoppers experience when faced with more choice than ever before. The good news is that having more options isn’t a problem. In fact, it’s an advantage. The first step is to know that there is dairy milk and non- dairy milk. For those who choose dairy milk, understanding the difference between Full Cream Milk , Filled Milk and age-appropriate milk products makes choosing the right option much easier. The key is understanding the purpose of each product. Once we understand those differences, choosing milk becomes less about guesswork and more about making informed decisions for ourselves and our families. After all, making informed nutrition decisions doesn’t begin when we pour milk into a cup. It begins with the knowledge and confidence to choose wisely. So, know your milk.
