items.title: Do Miracles Really Happen?
items.description: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube Carlos Eire arrived in Miami at age 11 in 1962, a refugee from Castro’s Cuba. Three years passed before his mother could join him, and he never saw his father again. This experience of dislocation profoundly shaped Eire’s work as a religious historian. In his latest book, They Flew , Eire looks at early modern reports of miracles. Drawing on his own experience of moving between cultures and worldviews, he tries to imagine himself into the minds of those who claimed to have witnessed levitations, bilocations, and other impossible occurrences, and he asks what we can learn by taking these reports seriously. David Brooks talks with Eire about magic, empathy, and the past as a foreign country. The following is a transcript of the episode: David Brooks: This is a conversation about radical empathy. We live in a polarized age, often with people whose modes of consciousness are utterly alien to our own. We hear someone spew a conspiracy theory or utter an opinion that seems monstrous, and we think: How on earth can they think that way? But being a good citizen in this sort of pluralistic society requires that kind of radical empathy. It means approaching those who are different with a willingness and an ability to stand in their standpoint, to enter into, at least a little, how they see the world. My guest is Carlos Eire, who has been trained by life to excel at this. When he was a boy, he was airlifted out of Cuba by parents who wanted to get him away from Castro’s revolution. He worked his way through college, got a Ph.D. here at Yale, where he is now a professor of history and religious studies, and began a double-barreled career. On the one hand, he entered into the minds of people living in the late Middle Ages, describing how they thought about death and demons. But alongside his academic work, Carlos also wrote two popular memoirs about his childhood, Waiting for Snow in Havana , which won a National Book Award, and Learning to Die in Miami . We’re going to talk about his travels across worldviews. We’re going to spend the bulk of this time on Carlos’s recent book, They Flew . We’re going to look at the testimonies of 16th- and 17th-century religious figures who claimed they could levitate. When I started reading the book, these claims seemed totally bonkers to me. But take the time to get inside their heads. Learn to see the world through alien eyes. I think you’ll find Carlos generously curious and gently wise. You may not leave this podcast thinking that humans can float into the ceiling, but I bet you’ll learn a few things about how to enter other people’s minds. Carlos Eire, welcome to The Permanent Questions . Thanks so much for crossing New Haven to get here. Carlos Eire: Thanks very much. Thank you very much for inviting me. Brooks: Let me try to lay out what I was hoping to accomplish. I sort of see this as about empathy, about encountering people who are completely unlike yourself and trying to see the world from their point of view. This strikes me as a pretty necessary skill to have in a pluralistic society like ours. I think for most of the time, we’ll talk about this book, They Flew , which is a history of the impossible and possibly the most audacious book I’ve ever read. We’ll get to that, but let’s start with the leaving of Cuba. The simplest way to introduce your story is: Tell me about Operation Peter Pan. Eire: Yes, it received that unfortunate name. It didn’t have a name for us who went through it. Between New Year’s Day 1961 and mid-October 1962, slightly over 14,000 unaccompanied Cuban children came to the US. The plan was always to reunite with our parents either there, if the dictatorship ended, or here. It was well-organized chaos. There’s no other way to describe it. The 14,000 of us were sent to 48 different states eventually. Brooks: And you were 11. Eire: I was 11 when I left, and I left with my brother, who was 14. We went through a series of foster homes in Miami at first because we didn’t have family, not yet. And my first foster family—beautiful family, I consider them saints, Norma and Lou Chait—were Jewish, and I thought I had it made now because, at that age, I didn’t like going to church. But no, they forced me to go to church, and gave me money to put into the collection basket. I learned English really fast because they had zero Spanish. So I ended up learning English and a few Yiddish words that I thought were English. I later discovered, when I moved to Bloomington, Illinois, that people didn’t understand what I was saying. Long story with many ins and outs. My brother and I also ended up spending nine months in a home for juvenile delinquents because there was no other place for us. It was supposed to be temporary, but they kind of forgot about us. Brooks: The regime was sending kids to the Soviet Union. Eire: Yes. And it had happened before in Spain during the Civil War. There were so many Spanish immigrants in Cuba, including my grandparents, who had a vivid memory of kids who never returned. So panic set in. And also for any male over 18—military service. Of course, these parents, my own included, it wouldn’t have crossed their minds that this would go on forever, that the regime would not collapse. That was a big surprise to everyone. There’s no fixed statistic on how many children left whose parents were unable to leave. Mine were among them. My mom, it took her three and a half years to finally come to the US, and my father never made it out. I never harbored ill feelings of any sort. Ever since day one, I have thanked my parents for making that choice. I know there are a few who couldn’t understand. But for me, it’s always been a sacrifice they made. Brooks: There was a famous book written in the ’80s by a guy named David Lowenthal called The Past Is a Foreign Country. His argument is: We have to understand these people are different than us. But his second point was that it’s not only that the past is a foreign country, but that our relationship to the past has changed. We think of it as a line. It’s moving forward; it’s not moving back. But in previous eras, you go to any art museum, they’re dressing Jesus in 16th-century garb. They’re mingling the eras. Time is going backward and forward. They have a different attitude. So does that concept—the past is a foreign country—is that something that resonates with you, humbles you, different views of the past? Eire: Yes. I mean, having that experience of getting off the plane at the Miami airport back in 1962, you know, experiencing all this. Definitely another country—I’m in another country. The past is a lot like that. There are things that are difficult to understand about the past, especially cultural dimensions that no longer exist. What people could say, what people did and could do, and not only that—the worldview. The worldview above everything else, because that’s what I have focused on in all of my work as a historian is the cultural-religious dimension, the worldview that changed in the 16th century. I did have, however, I thought, an advantage over my American colleagues when it came to studying the Protestant Reformation, which was the revolution. I understood it as a revolution. And I saw many things happening in the early years of the Protestant Reformation that to me seemed only slightly different from the present. So it’s almost like I was a time traveler, right? And it was not a foreign country to me, for instance, to learn about the consistory in Calvin’s Geneva, which policed everyone’s behavior. I know what that’s like. And then when I went on to study the Spanish Inquisition, same thing. I’ve lived through this. People being ostracized for thinking incorrectly about some minor point—I’ve lived through that. That was not a foreign country to me. But when it comes to big items like belief in miracles, belief in witches, belief in demonic possession, all the supernatural stuff, of course it’s changed tremendously, but not entirely. The paradoxical challenge every historian faces is that something might look very similar to you, but it ends up not being all that similar. For instance, I spent a long time reading last wills and testaments from 16th-century Madrid. And I found one that I said, “Oh, they’re just like us.” This woman was bequeathing her little precious dog to so and so. But everyone was requesting hundreds of masses for their soul, sometimes thousands of masses. I even had a few last wills and testaments where the individual was listing as their only heir their soul. Brooks: Oh, really? Eire: Yes. And it sounds funny in English: The soul was the sole heir. But honestly, yes. Including one, I said, “This is a totally different world.” One priest who put it into his will. He says, “I know my family’s going to object, but they never did anything for me. I did this all on my own. This is my money.” And then I thought, “Well, now I’m back in this world.” So you get these mixed messages. It is very, very gratifying to find traces of human emotion like that lady willing her dog to her friend. It was a friend that she trusted. Brooks: I read that in the Middle Ages, and your period is sort of in the late Middle Ages, the emotions were more on the surface. I don’t know if this is measurable. But when they were in joy, they were in ecstasy. When they were in despair—the emotional register was much more vivacious than ours. Eire: It could be. Of course it depends on time and place and everything else that’s going on around people. But yes, I think that’s true. There was a lot of violence. A student of mine ended up doing his dissertation on violence in 16th-century Spain, looking at a very small town where all the records survived. People were fighting, like physically fighting, all the time. Then I understood why I had so many wills from people who were on their deathbed with head injuries. These emotions in the past, in one way, had to be dulled much more than with us. For instance, executions were public. And it wasn’t a nice execution. It was usually people being beheaded or hung or tortured. People lived through this. We would think immediately: Well, everyone there watching this is going to be severely traumatized . And perhaps they were, right? Brooks: They seem pretty happy in the accounts. Eire: People are cheering and clapping. Another world, another country. Absolutely. Brooks: This is one I’ve always wondered about. You’ve written about death, as you said. There’s an argument that you occasionally hear that so parents lost so many children that the loss of a child was not as emotionally crushing as it is for moderns. I sort of find that hard to believe. Eire: I do too. I think that’s somebody in the present saying, “It must have been that way. They had to.” But no, I don’t think so. We have plenty of evidence from diaries. There’s one diary that’s a tanner in Barcelona, 17th century, who lived through a plague in Barcelona. All his children died. And you can tell in the diary, it really hit him. Also, bringing it to the present, he actually wrote in his diary that the one child who survived was his least favorite. And why did it have to be that way? Brooks: There’s an argument that you raise in the book, though I don’t think you endorse it, that all these beliefs—whether in miracles, demonic possession, all that kind of stuff—it was functional for the period; it served some function. You quote a historian, Keith Thomas: “Belief in magic and miracles was an absolute necessity in premodern times due to ‘a preoccupation with the explanation and relief of human misfortune.’” Life was so hazardous that believing in all this stuff was part of the way they handled the hazardousness of their lives. Eire: And I think there’s truth in that, but I don’t think that’s all that’s going on. I was trained to be a functionalist. If there’s anything weird happening, anything supernatural happening, you just don’t go there. You bracket that. You don’t ask the question: Well, was this person really floating in the air or not? You analyze what function that belief served in that culture. But I have rebelled against my functionalist training. Brooks: Yeah, I’ll say big time. We get now to They Flew , and I started this book—it’s really a story of testimonies about levitation and bilocation, which is a person saying they were in two places at once. And I started this book with, I’m sure, the normal attitude you have encountered everywhere. One, people don’t levitate. It’s all a myth. And two, I’m not that interested. Why should I care about something that didn’t happen? Then I start reading the book, and I’m reading the testimonies and entering that other world. My mind is blown. If I were talking to somebody and reading testimonies like this in a current U.S. court of law, I would think they were pretty compelling. So describe to us what those testimonies were like and what the circumstances were. Eire: As a historian, I would’ve felt immensely uncomfortable arguing in any way that these things really happened if I didn’t have the right kind of testimonies. It’s all based on testimonies. Actually, for this time period that I work in, the early modern period, we have an advantage over the medieval period in that—especially in the Catholic world, the part of the world that remained Catholic—the process for identifying saints was made more rigorous in this time period. So the canonization process, which involves several sets of inquests, interviewing the people who knew this person, they include a section on miracles. But every answer that anyone gives in that inquest is sworn testimony, and the penalty’s not just a fine or some time behind bars. It’s hell, for lying. Most of the testimonies—not most, in some cases just many—come from very, very religious people, even clerics and nuns. So are these people going to perjure themselves, if they believe in hell? Brooks: These were not just unlettered people. Some of these testimonies are from the intellectual elite. And they’re saying, “Oh, so and so levitated.” Or they’re describing their own experiences, and there are tons of witnesses. I still don’t believe they levitated, but the testimony is … Eire: Well, we’re faced with a conundrum, which can be explained away in various ways. I’ve read one analysis of Joseph of Cupertino, this flying friar, the guy who spent more time in the air than anyone else in history: He was an acrobat. He had trained his muscles so well, like a gymnast, that he could make these great leaps. But no, he was suspended in the air, for heaven’s sake. And there are fakes. I have a whole section in the book about frauds, people who were caught faking all of this. Because as I said, it’s always been a case that people can fake these things. Magicians fake it all the time on stage. But faking it outdoors in the 16th or 17th century, that’s a little harder to do without ropes and pulleys or wires or anything. So we’re left with these testimonies, and what do we do with these testimonies? They are part of the past. Almost every time I’ve spoken about this book in public, the question comes up. I’ve had other historians bring it up, and other historians who share my point of view that we should take these testimonies very seriously. There is definitely a correlation throughout history, including the present—the correlation between the matrix of belief that a culture has and the frequency with which these anomalous phenomena occur. Brooks: What do you mean by that: “the matrix of belief”? What do you mean? Eire: If, let’s say, belief in levitation specifically is prevalent in a culture, you’re going to get more levitations. If belief in levitations is laughed at, as it is in our culture, you’re gonna have fewer. The same goes for any miraculous event. Brooks: I found the most compelling set of testimonies came from Teresa of Ávila. So could you tell us who she was and how she levitated? Eire: Teresa of Ávila, 16th century, was a Carmelite nun who from her 40s on had continuous ecstatic religious experiences, mystical ecstasies. Some of them involved levitation. She is one of the few levitators who has given us first-person accounts of what it feels like and what’s going on. So we have great detail on that from her end, from the personal end. Plus we have all these eyewitnesses, which were the nuns that she lived with and people who visited the convent, who testify to these incredible levitations. And she actually resisted these levitations. That’s another curious twist in her story. She begged God to stop it. She came right out and said to God, “Why are you doing this? What purpose does this serve?” And they stopped. She tells us in her autobiography they stopped. But that part of her autobiography she ended in 1562. The levitations came back again, with less frequency, but they came back again. She doesn’t write about it. She doesn’t complain about these. She’s complaining about the early ones. Brooks: I think her testimony is not like, “Look at me and what I did.” Her testimony is just like, “Here’s what it felt like.” I’m gonna read a few just so people get a sense: “At the highest point of rapture, one will neither see nor hear nor perceive. None of the soul’s faculties are able to perceive or know what is taking place.” So she’s describing that something goes blank. And then the resisting: “When I tried to resist these raptures, it seemed to me that I was being lifted up by a force beneath my feet so powerful that I know nothing to which I can compare it, for it came with much greater intensity than any other spiritual experience. I felt I was being torn to shreds, for it is a mighty struggle.” So these are physically demanding, arduous things. And then she’s bothered because she’s turning into a little celebrity for floating around the rooms, and this is the last thing she wants. And so she said, “There was no way of avoiding them, even in public. And then the persecutions and the murmurings follow. Even though the soul wants to be free from fears, she is never free of them because so many people foist them on her.” One day she’s frying eggs. She’s got a frying pan, she’s frying eggs, and suddenly she’s up in the ceiling. This of course is dangerous for her because the church could decide she’s demonically possessed, because levitation can either be a sign of your holiness or demonic possession. So this is a maximally perilous thing, and she does not wanna be talking about it. I think they force her. Eire: She’s walking a tightrope every time she went up. I have found some common threads linking all the levitators from this period who are eventually declared to be the genuine thing—that this is divine; this is not demonic. One of them is what Teresa describes, this cataleptic seizure, where you lose your senses, just vanish, and you don’t sense anything that’s going on around you, and then your body stiffens in whatever position. Sometimes these levitators go up, they’re praying on their knees, and they go up, and their knees are bent. And people actually try to unbend them, and they report that they can’t. I had a conversation here at the Yale Divinity School some months ago with a neurologist about all this stuff. It’s a very interesting conversation because he pointed to this spot on his head, and he says, “I can tell you exactly where these nuns are having these experiences.” And yes, you can pathologize as much as you want. If it were just a person telling you, “I felt this,” then it would be entirely explained. No more questions asked. But to have people say, “We saw this happen,” and to have it under oath, not just once but multiple times—then I think you need some other angle. You need to take this from another angle or another perspective and say that something is going on here that we, in our culture, none of us have been prepared to accept as a real possibility. Brooks: One of the beauties of the book is your first job as a historian is not to judge. It’s just to witness. Just look. What are they talking about? How are they thinking about this? And that part is very admirable, but I’m trying to picture you working on this book, taking these testimonies seriously of levitation. And I have found that the biggest bias in media, maybe in the academy too, is not a left or right bias. It’s: What do people at dinner parties that people like me go to talk about? And if you have a category outside what people like me talk about, you are rejected. So as you’re writing this book, taking this stuff seriously, you must have been aware a lot of people are gonna think you’re crazy. Eire: Yes, but I’m used to that. And actually, back to the first part of our talk, I’m used to it because being in academia, for decades, if I could do it, I would hide the fact that I was Cuban from my colleagues. Because every time I said I was Cuban, I would get a little speech about how wonderful the revolution was. And if I said anything that was negative, all of a sudden, you’re not okay. You’re not okay. So I was used to that. Also, any person who has a religious life of any kind, the dominant culture, it does not accept your way of living as normal with a capital N . So you get used to that after a while. But having people dislike what I have to say is something that I’m used to. Brooks: You write at one point in They Flew : “Ask any historian why they write the kind of history they do, and if they are honest, they will tell you that when all is said and done, the history they write has everything to do with their life story, their yearnings, and their obsessions. This author is no different.” What does that mean? How do I interpret your decision to go into late medieval history? Eire: All my work as a historian has focused, in different ways, on the same subject, which is my obsession, which is, at bottom, the marrow of religion, as far as belief is concerned. There is some other dimension that is, for lack of a better term, more real than this, from which this dimension is derived. Brooks: And are you testing that proposition, or are you convinced by primordial faith that this proposition is true, and you’re trying to see how it works out? Eire: When I started out, and even now, I’ve had my ups and downs about that visceral kind of affirmation. That it’s not rational or purely intellectual. So that’s been constant, but it’s gone up and down. But the older I’ve become, the more that that has seemed very real to me. But the fact is, yes, belief is different from knowledge that you acquire through normal cognitive processes. Which is another reason that—I’ve also been obsessed looking at the phenomenon of mysticism. It’s the ecstasies that drew me to this subject first. It’s the claim, the existential claim people make to have experienced something other, with a capital O . Brooks: You can argue about whether people are flying up in the air, but there really are mystics. We all know people who have a mystical tongue or a mystical sense that I will never experience, but I know them and I see them, and I watch them. Eire: It’s the same with, let’s say, a musical virtuoso or an athletic virtuoso. That’s what at this advanced age of mine I’ve come to realize—that gifts are unevenly spread. Religion is one of these. There are people who just are spiritually gifted. And there are some who are spiritually blind and deaf, who just can’t even conceive of. I’ve often used this in my mysticism class, the believability of any mystic’s accounts of what it’s like to experience the divine. They all tell you the same thing, at least in the Christian tradition, but also in other religious traditions: “I can’t explain it to you.” It’s like explaining color to a blind person. How do you go about explaining color? No, it’s just another perception, another way of perceiving. What I still find fascinating is when those experiences which go beyond normal cognition have some physical impact on the person having it. Brooks: Yeah, I, I’ve seen friends who are—they’re moving, they’re kneeling. They’re not even thinking about it. They don’t know you were looking at them. They’re speaking sort of in tongues or some sort of other language. I don’t think it proves a belief in God, but it proves the existence of some sort of spiritual faculty that people have. I wanted to talk about the context in which Teresa’s living and a lot of the people in this 16th-, 17th-century period. This is a moment when science is beginning to take off, and you get Descartes, and I suppose go a little later you get Newton. This is reason and science taking off. Technology’s beginning to move up. It’s exactly this moment, as you make the point in the book, that these mystical experiences and these levitations begin to hit back. And it could be that there’s just intense pressure. They’ve hit a civilizational fork in the road, and they’re either gonna go off in the rationalist direction, or they’re gonna stay the way they were. And the crass way to put it, which I don’t want to reduce it just to this, is if you’re a Carmelite nun, you think, “Okay, you guys got calculus. That’s impressive, but we fly around the room.” Eire: I can’t argue against this way of looking at things. It makes sense, yes. I think it’s highly probable that you have this heightened sensibility toward the miraculous as a response not just to emerging science, but more immediately, at first, the Protestant Reformation, which is denying that all of these things are divine. But then along comes the scientific revolution. And yes, it is a natural response that people focus more intensely on these things. And as I said before, there seems to be this very common linkage between the matrix of belief and the frequency of these things happening. That’s a very solid, very rational argument, but it doesn’t explain everything. It just doesn’t. If in fact these things are happening and continued to happen, albeit with less frequency, you’re still dealing with a phenomenon. As I have discovered lately, there’s a word now being used to describe human beings who claim to have encountered nonhuman intelligence, and that word is experiencer . That’s also used for mystics. So in essence, a mystic telling you, “I understood the Trinity perfectly, but I can’t tell you” has the same trouble being believed as somebody who says, “This gray alien walked into my hotel room last night.” Brooks: There’s a famous episode which is sort of this clash. Rene Descartes, he’s early 17th century, he is actually a believer, but he decides he’s gonna sweep away all this tradition and knowledge that’s built up, and he’s gonna start from scratch. He’s gonna use pure reason, just logical, follow one step after another, and he makes sure he’s shielded from emotion. God forbid he should love somebody. And he’s trying to build up the whole edifice of human knowledge. And at exactly the same time, this other guy in France, Blaise Pascal, takes a look at what Descartes is doing and immediately hates him. Blaise Pascal is no random humanist. He was one of the greatest mathematicians to ever live. He was a technologist. He built a sort of early calculating machine. He was a scientist. He studied vacuums. So he had scientific rigor on his side, and he was saying, “I’m not against Descartes’s reason, but I have many other forms of knowledge that I use to understand the world.” The “spirit of genius” and the “spirit of finesse,” I think he called it. And he famously said, “The heart has reasons that reason knows not of.” And so he’s saying to Descartes, “You’re taking away other ways of knowing . ” And I think the clinching argument—it’s so amazing he understood this right away. We’re at this civilizational fork in the road. He says the problem with rationalism is not its admiration for reason, but its failure to recognize any other kind of knowledge. He’s saying, “You’re amputating me.” He’s talking out of his own experience of how he has studied the world. Eire: Plus he had a mystical experience. Brooks: Famously at the Night of Fire. Eire: Sewn into the lining of his coat: God of Abraham, God of Isaac, God of Jacob, not of the philosophers. This distinction being made between these two forms of cognition. I’m so glad you brought up Pascal because he’s a contemporary. But there’s so many. When you’re dealing with the past—again, a different country—you find anomalous synchronicities all the time. One of the witnesses to St. Joseph of Cupertino’s levitations was a Saxon prince, Johann Friedrich of Saxony. And not just any Saxony, the Saxony that Luther had been part of. For some reason, he’s in Italy, and nobody has figured out what he was doing there. But he sees Joseph of Cupertino up in the air and he converts to Catholicism. Johann Friedrich. Oh my God. This is the same man who hired Leibniz as his librarian. Did he and Leibniz ever meet in the hallway, so to speak? And to talk about these things? A little thought experiment that I engage in my book: Yes, Newton and Joseph Cupertino walked the Earth, the same time. What if Newton had taken time off and done the grand tour and run into Joseph Cupertino? They could have. Yes, but they didn’t. They just didn’t. And Newton spent much of his later life trying to figure out the law of prophecy. Brooks: So we’re talking about this crucial time in Western history at least, where science is moving, and faith is moving in a different way. It seems to me you could look over periods of scientific advance—faith rises to respond. And so the period I know best is the late 19th century, the Industrial Revolution. You’ve got these machines. In the late 19th century, Henry Adams, who was in the same family as John Quincy Adams and John Adams, he goes to a bunch of world fairs. And he sees what they were obsessed with in the Chicago World’s Fair. He writes a chapter in his book, which is more famous than the rest of—well, the book’s pretty famous too, called The Education of Henry Adams —but the chapter is called “The Dynamo and the Virgin.” The Virgin, he says—different eras in time have different power sources. And in the 13th century, the Virgin was a tremendous power source in Europe, and we get all these cathedrals that they were wanting to buy ’cause the Virgin was their power source. And he says, “That’s going away.” And he writes in that chapter—humans have a tendency to worship power sources, and people are gonna start worshiping machines. It’s not clear what he thinks about it, but at the exact same moment, there are a lot of other people, or roughly in that industrial period, who really mined it. And then the part I hadn’t clued in until reading your book, ’cause you mentioned this, at exactly this moment, late 19th century, a lot of the world goes gaga over seances. People you wouldn’t expect, like Arthur Conan Doyle, the founder of Sherlock Holmes, Mr. Rational. You mention Abraham Lincoln’s wife. A lot of serious people were sitting around doing seances and Ouija boards and stuff like that. Eire: And that’s kind of the tip of the iceberg because this is the same period that gives us the Latter-day Saints, the Millerites, and eventually the Jehovah’s Witnesses. Theosophy, which becomes immensely popular. Brooks: Explain what that is. Eire: Theosophy is a blend of Western occult mysticism with basically Hinduism and Buddhism. And it was enormously popular, here in the United States, but also throughout the world. The American Theosophical Society, which for a while was based in Philadelphia, sent missionaries all around the world. I learned this from a dissertation I read back when I was at the University of Virginia. Otherwise, I would not have found this fact, which I find fascinating: The two most successful missions that the American Theosophical Society had were Brazil and Cuba. But they’re also immensely popular throughout Europe. Anyway, the list could be longer of all these other things. Arthur Conan Doyle came here to New Haven during his American tour and spoke at Woolsey Hall. Brooks: Which is the big hall here on campus. Eire: Yes. The big auditorium. On spirit photography. And it was packed. Standing room only. This spiritualism only intensifies during and right after the First World War. Brooks: That makes sense because there’s so many dead people. Eire: Especially all the dead young people, and parents desperate to come to terms with this. The Society for Psychic Studies is established in London in the late 19th century. There’s such a long list of other things that emerge at this very same time, occultism and everything else. This is because, as I see it—Pascal’s complaint, which is personal, can have a social and cultural dimension to it. When you take away belief in something that has ultimate meaning in another dimension other than this—because everybody’s body will give out on them and they will die, right? When you take that away—for lack of a better term, and I hate this term, disenchantment —you disenchant the world, the world will try to re-enchant itself. And it always does so, or often does so in very weird ways. Sometimes in very, very bad ways. The French Revolution. The Bolshevik Revolution. The Third Reich. If you look at those three, they are aggressive attempts to re-enchant the world differently. They have religious symbols. They have feasts. They have holidays. They have rituals. You name it, but the ultimate thing is the revolution. Brooks: The Marxist revolutions also laid claim to science too,though they were clearly secular religions. Eire: But they still have the trappings of a religion and require belief in an orthodoxy. And in some kind of apocalyptic future, right? Brooks: This brings me to today. So we’re in the world of AI now, and tech, and Elon Musk, and if you go to the Silicon Valley, they also have a kind of religion. They worship a god, which is intelligence. They believe in sin, which is inefficiency. They believe in moral progress, which is optimization. They believe in eternal life, which is transhumanism. You can download your brain on a computer and live forever. And so they’ve got it all going on, even though they would deny that they are religious, but it looks very much like a religion serving assertive existential longings. Eire: And given human instinct, that seems to be part of human history, that whenever something or someone comes along that seems to have immense power, or a combination of immense intelligence and immense power, people will venerate this. That’s one of the threats of AI that doesn’t get much attention, but what I think is a real possibility is that if, in fact, we get artificial intelligence, which by the way, can also be called nonhuman intelligence—if we got one that’s super intelligent enough, of course you’re going to have people who will not only use it, but have their whole lives directed by it. Brooks: You mentioned something that stuck in my head from a few minutes ago: that you don’t like the word disenchantment . Why is that? Eire: It’s sprinkled with fairy dust. The word in English enchantment has too much of an emotional baggage attached to it. It’s got an emotional dimension to it. But what happens when you take religion away is not disenchantment, not in that sense. It’s something much more aggressive. And what you lose is not emotion. What you lose is precisely, as Pascal complained, this other dimension. So that’s why I don’t like it. And especially too, I have personal reasons to complain because the subject I’ve been working on throughout my entire career falls into the category of disenchantment of the world. But all the definitions of enchantment or disenchantment that have been thrown at me—some of them ridiculous. For instance, may he rest in peace, Robert Scribner, a historian of the same time period, who said, “Protestants really didn’t disenchant the world, because they still had rituals.” I said, “What do you mean? Is that your sole criterion for enchantment or disenchantment? Of course people are going to have rituals. Government have rituals, right?” So it’s a very weak word. I wish there were a better word that people agreed on. This fuzzy word started to be used in 1930, when Talcott Parsons translated Max Weber and his phrase “Entzauberung der Welt,” with the word zauber right in the middle, which means “magic” in German. And he was very clear throughout several of his texts—he meant magic. Brooks: So you mentioned Max Weber. He wrote this process of rationalization, which led, I think in one translation, to what we call the “iron cage,” which is where we humans are stuck in this iron cage. And as a result, people’s spiritual lives shrivel, and in his words they become, I think it was, “specialists without spirit, sensualists without heart.” And I think that’s real. I live in Washington. I’m surrounded by specialists without spirit, sensualists without heart. Eire: His word for that was Entzauberung , not disenchantment. Brooks: Okay. And what, how would you translate that? Eire: Zauber is “magic.” Brooks: I see. Eire: Right? Which he also said in one sentence, that Entzauberung means taking away magie , M-A-G-I-E, which was the learned German word for magic . What he meant was that there’s no transcendent other dimension. And he also spoke of prophets. The only way that the world can be enchanted again is through prophets. And by prophets, he meant something like mystics, who actually have a real existential connection to something larger that can then convince other people that there’s more to life than this table and this microphone. He also spoke of the choices that people are left in this—let’s stay with disenchantment—disenchanted world. The choices that people are left with, it’s basically kind of a polytheism. Where you have to choose between different gods. It goes back to this insight that is a constant throughout the Christian tradition, this realization that human beings have an innate need for meaning. And that meaning has to be ultimate, not just proximate. It has to be ultimate. So we do our damnedest to make it up. Or as Pascal said, we do our damnedest to keep ourselves distracted so that we don’t look at the abyss that lies just a few feet away. Brooks: I think that distraction’s a key point. You can go through life not thinking about this stuff. There are two things that seem to be going on. I have a friend and former New York Times colleague, Ross Douthat, who argued that as society secularizes, you don’t get atheism; you get the strangest religions you can think of. There’s a book by a woman named Tara Isabella Burton called Strange Rites , where she details all these new religions that are popping up as people try to find some meaning somewhere. And this reminds me, I hadn’t made the connection to that 19th-century upstate New York— Eire: The burned-over district. Brooks: —when all these new religions were popping up all over the place. But then I think there’s other things going on, which is there really is a dis—well, I don’t wanna use that word; you’ll reach across the table and punch me—but there is a materialistic mentality that is definitely more prevalent today than in the 17th century. And I think that’s sad. So I guess my question for you is: When you’re writing all this stuff, are you partly motivated by a disquiet with the present? Eire: Oh, definitely. Most definitely. Yes. I’m very disquieted, and I’ve been disquieted for quite some time, since childhood. But my present baggage, let’s put it that way, has to do with the way in which one can be so easily silenced or ridiculed for merely suggesting that something else should be taken seriously. That’s enough to put you in the category of an alien abductee. David Brooks: The book came out, I think, in ’23. How has the reaction response been, both from the professional historical community and from the wider public? Eire: Well, the professional historical community is so slow. Our book reviews sometimes take two to three years. So I have yet to see very many reviews in professional journals. But in other venues, the response has been overwhelmingly positive. There’ve been a couple of nasty book reviews. I expected them. One of them with a beautiful sentence: “This is a deeply unserious book.” Brooks: That’s a compliment where I come from. Eire: Another reviewer found it necessary, for whatever reason, to bring up the fact that I was Cuban, and therefore I’m credulous and very fond of magical realism. Brooks: You’re Gabriel García Márquez. Eire: Yes, I am, like all Latin Americans. Yeah. You know, we’re all a little ... Brooks: That’s why we love you. Now I have two final topics. One is, and I wanted to ask you about this—you say there’s a supernatural mentality and there’s a material mentality. But you introduce this concept that there’s also a third way of believing in the middle there, which you say is a “vast polymorphous, variegated middle between these two extreme poles, abounding in myriad attitudes and convictions.” As a natural temperamental moderate, that sounds good to me. Eire: And I think that’s basically my position. When you’re faced with unknowns, what do you do? How do you make up your mind? I just thought of this, and your question prompted this to appear—I take the same attitude to quantum entanglement and the Big Bang that I do to these phenomena. Until I see somebody up in the air and say, “Yes, I’m seeing this,” I can’t say I’ve experienced it, in the same way that you can say about any kind of religious experience, “Yes, I have experienced this.” I’ve been to many religious services where I have been so transported, I guess is a good way to put it. I’m not there in the room. I mean, I know I’m there, but I’m not there. And some of them have been very odd moments too. In houses of worship other than Catholic. It’s happened. That’s one thing. But seeing somebody up in the air, though. But quantum entanglement, what do you do with this? And what do you do with the latest images from the Webb telescope telling us that the Big Bang may be something else? Brooks: The scientists who I know, whom I admire, some of them are just arrogantly dismissive of all spiritual experience. I say, “Well, you explain how consciousness emerged from the brain, then I’ll take your arrogance as somewhat earned. Or you explain what happened before the Big Bang. You can’t do that. You explain quantum entanglement.” You can’t explain any of this stuff. The existence of the universe and consciousness, which is our primary ways to understand the world, if you can’t explain these two things—these are the two biggest things in our world. Eire: If I were younger, I think this is the area I would dive into next. All this work that’s being done on mind and consciousness, which is, in fact, a connecting point, a nexus, very natural nexus, religion and science. But I have so much reading to do. Can’t do it now. Brooks: So many years have been wasted trying to solve the consciousness problem. Okay, the final question. All of our conversation has been leading up to one question: Did they fly? Eire: Yes. And I don’t mean to put any qualifiers on this. I’m willing to take that testimony as one would in a court of law, although there’s no physical evidence. That’s the one difference. There’s no murder weapon, let’s say. But let me put it this way: I think it’s highly, highly likely, especially since we have reports. What I find very annoying, though, extremely annoying, is that cameras and film have been in existence for well over a century. Brooks: That’s the obvious rejoinder to your belief. What’s your answer? Eire: Right. Where is it? Where is it? Some television show tried to trick me, said, “We have film of somebody levitating. Would you watch it?” They were doing this live. And, yeah, it was obvious this person was spinning on a highwire. I said, “Well, you’re not showing what’s at the other end here. Is there another tree or another pole?” They said, “Yeah, we didn’t wanna tell you ahead of time. We just wanted your reaction.” Brooks: I must say, I still am not quite there where you are, but I’m struck by how much in our popular culture, how much flying there is. Superman is flying. Harry Potter is flying on his broom. There’s a lot of flying. Look, we accept this so easily when we think it’s a superhero story or fiction. Eire: Well, we have maglev trains. It’s not like this is physically impossible. You can actually physically levitate small frogs with sound waves. Brooks: Oh really? Eire: Yes, that’s been done. Brooks: It’s very unpleasant for the frogs. Eire: Well, coins—everybody has seen coins levitate. But you can take a little tiny frog, and with acoustic, levitation can take place. So it’s not physiologically or physically impossible. One of my early talks on the subject long, long before the book came out, there was a doctor in the audience. I always love the first question because it’s always the most troublesome: Did these people have a lot of iron in their diets, by the way? Maybe they were magnets in the room. Brooks: That’s a lot of iron. Eire: I said, “No, I don’t think so.” Yeah. I don’t think so. Brooks: Carlos, I really appreciate your taking the time, and I really enjoyed our conversation. Eire: Oh, my pleasure. Brooks: I’m hoping that people come away with their mind expanded, but also come away with—when in life we encounter people whose political views, religious views, whatever views seem crazy to us, we pause and we say, “Where are you coming from? Let me try to see the world from your eyes.” And that strikes me as the essence of democracy. Eire: It is, and it’s essential for survival. Brooks: I thought one of the most interesting moments in my conversation with Carlos is when I asked him right at the end, “Did they fly?” And he flat out said, “Yes, they did.” Think of the intellectual courage it takes to say that. A lot of people are going to think that’s ridiculous, but he’s a man of his convictions. He thinks supernatural realities are real. He’s also a man who’s done the work. He spent the years in the archives reading all these testimonies, so he’s got some substance behind what he’s thinking. I personally am not quite convinced. I think if human beings had the capacity to levitate, then we’d find one video of it, or somebody would be doing it today. But I believe that the people who described their levitation sincerely believed they were flying, just the way I might sincerely believe I’m driving down the New Jersey Turnpike. And how did they believe this? I don’t know. But I respect the fact that they did it. When it comes to humans, variability is the rule. We’ve got a lot of different mindsets out there, and people hold sincere beliefs that seem bonkers to the rest of us, but are probably worthy of our respect. Thanks so much for joining us for this week’s conversation with Carlos Eire. The Permanent Questions is produced and edited by The Atlantic , in partnership with Yale University. New episodes of The Permanent Questions come out on Sundays. You can subscribe on The Atlantic ’s YouTube page, Apple, Spotify, or wherever you get your podcasts. If you want to support this work and the work of my colleagues, you can subscribe to the publication at TheAtlantic.com/Listener . See you next week.

items.title: Conakry : le ministre Bourouno lance la 3è phase du concours d’accès à l’ENA de Guinée
items.description: L’École nationale d’administration (ENA) de Guinée a franchi une nouvelle étape dans le processus de recrutement des élèves de sa toute première promotion. Ce dimanche, 570 candidats, présélectionnés à l’issue des épreuves de questionnaires à choix multiples (QCM), ont pris part à la troisième phase du concours, organisée à l’Université Gamal Abdel Nasser de Conakry. À l’issue de cette étape, 240 candidats seront retenus pour poursuivre leur parcours au sein de cette institution appelée à contribuer à la transformation de l’administration publique guinéenne. Présent sur le site pour lancer les épreuves, le ministre de la Modernisation de l’Administration et de la Fonction publique, Faya François Bourouno, a insisté sur la rigueur du processus de sélection, le respect de l’égalité des chances et la recherche du mérite. Pour le gouvernement, la mise en place de cette école constitue un levier de formation de cadres capables de répondre aux exigences d’une administration publique plus performante et davantage tournée vers les citoyens. « Nous sommes en train de recruter les élèves de la première promotion du diplôme de l’École nationale d’administration (ENA). Conformément au protocole qui encadre les programmes de formation, nous accordons une grande rigueur au processus d’élaboration des programmes, notamment à celui de la sélection des participants au programme du diplôme », a expliqué le ministre. Selon le ministre Bourouno, le concours repose sur un processus de sélection structuré en quatre étapes. Après l’examen des dossiers de candidature et les épreuves de QCM organisées il y a quelques semaines, les candidats admissibles ont été convoqués ce dimanche pour les épreuves écrites. Une quatrième étape est prévue dans le dispositif de sélection. Cette troisième phase vise notamment à évaluer les capacités rédactionnelles des candidats, en complément de leurs aptitudes à répondre aux questions à choix multiples. Un critère que le ministre juge essentiel pour les futurs élèves fonctionnaires appelés à intégrer l’administration publique. « Il y a la capacité à répondre aux questions sous forme de QCM, mais nous voulons également tester et évaluer les capacités rédactionnelles des futurs élèves fonctionnaires de l’École nationale d’administration », a-t-il précisé. Au-delà des connaissances théoriques, les autorités entendent ainsi s’assurer que les futurs élèves disposent des aptitudes nécessaires pour suivre une formation exigeante et, à terme, exercer des responsabilités au sein des services publics. Le mérite et l’égalité des chances au cœur du recrutement Lors de sa visite, le ministre a également vérifié les conditions matérielles et organisationnelles mises en place pour le bon déroulement des épreuves. Il s’est dit satisfait du dispositif observé dans les salles d’examen, estimant que les dispositions prises permettaient aux candidats de composer dans des conditions appropriées. « Nous sommes à la recherche du mérite, à travers le processus de sélection. Nous savons également que l’école reposera sur l’excellence et la rigueur dans tout le processus d’enseignement », a-t-il déclaré. Pour garantir le bon déroulement de cette phase, plusieurs mesures administratives, logistiques, sécuritaires et communicationnelles ont été mobilisées. Elles portent notamment sur la constitution des dossiers, l’information des candidats, la mise à disposition des salles et la sécurisation du centre d’examen. À cette occasion, François Bourouno a salué l’appui du rectorat de l’Université Gamal Abdel Nasser de Conakry, ainsi que celui du ministère de l’Enseignement supérieur et de la Recherche scientifique, pour la mise à disposition du cadre ayant accueilli les candidats. Une école au service de la qualité de l’administration publique Si l’accès au diplôme de l’ENA est soumis à une sélection rigoureuse, le ministre a tenu à rappeler que l’établissement a vocation à proposer des programmes diversifiés et à rester ouvert à différents profils. Il a toutefois souligné que le programme diplômant destiné à former les futurs cadres de l’administration nécessite un niveau d’exigence particulier. « L’école est ouverte à tout le monde. C’est pourquoi nous avons diversifié les programmes. Cependant, le programme conduisant au diplôme de l’ENA doit être mis en œuvre avec toute la rigueur nécessaire », a-t-il indiqué. À travers ce recrutement, les autorités ambitionnent de constituer une première promotion répondant aux exigences de formation, de compétence et de professionnalisme attendues dans la fonction publique. L’objectif final, selon le ministre, est d’améliorer la qualité des prestations administratives et de faciliter l’accès des citoyens aux services publics. « La finalité recherchée est de faire en sorte que le service public offert aux citoyens soit un service de qualité et accessible à tous », a conclu le ministre. La sélection des 240 futurs élèves constituera ainsi une étape déterminante dans le lancement des activités de formation de l’ENA. Au-delà du concours, l’enjeu est de préparer des cadres capables de contribuer à la modernisation de l’État et à l’amélioration durable du fonctionnement de l’administration guinéenne. items.title: Israël : des milliers de manifestants contre Netanyahou à trois jours des législatives
items.description: Des milliers d'Israeliens ont defile le 24 octobre a Tel Aviv contre le gouvernement du Premier ministre Benjamin Netanyahou, a trois jours d'elections legislatives qui s'annoncent serrees. La manifestation, organisee par le Conseil d'Octobre, un collectif de familles de victimes et d'otages de l'attaque du 7 octobre 2023, visait notamment a reclamer des comptes sur les defaillances securitaires qui ont permis cette attaque du Hamas, la plus meurtriere de l'histoire d'Israel. Les manifestants se sont rassembles sur la place des Otages, devenue depuis le debut de la guerre a Gaza un lieu emblematique des mobilisations en faveur du retour des personnes enlevees lors de l'attaque. Le Conseil d'Octobre demande la mise en place d'une commission d'enquete independante, une initiative jusqu'ici refusee par le gouvernement Netanyahou. Les principales figures de l'opposition avaient annonce leur participation au rassemblement. Parmi elles figuraient le centriste Gadi Eisenkot, le chef de l'opposition Yaïr Lapid, son allie Naftali Bennett, l'ancien ministre de la Defense Avigdor Liberman et le dirigeant du parti Les Democrates, Yaïr Golan. Ces responsables se sont engages a creer une commission d'enquete en cas de victoire electorale. Des elections sous haute tension Le scrutin du 27 octobre, le premier depuis l'attaque du 7 octobre 2023, est largement presente comme un test politique pour Benjamin Netanyahou, au pouvoir depuis 2022. Selon les derniers sondages autorises a etre publies la veille, le bloc du Premier ministre etait credite de 50 sieges, contre 52 pour le bloc d'opposition constitue autour de Gadi Eisenkot. Ces projections restaient eloignees des 61 sieges necessaires pour obtenir une majorite a la Knesset. Au-dela des defaillances securitaires, la campagne electorale est marquee par les consequences de la guerre a Gaza, les tensions regionales et les critiques internationales visant la politique israelienne, notamment en Cisjordanie occupee. Certains electeurs de l'opposition esperent qu'une alternance permettra d'ameliorer les relations d'Israel avec la communaute internationale. Benjamin Netanyahou a egalement suscite des reactions apres avoir evoque le 23 octobre la preparation d'un plan visant a developper une economie alternative pour contourner d'eventuelles sanctions internationales, notamment dans le secteur bancaire. Il a cite la blockchain parmi les pistes envisagees. Gadi Eisenkot a tourne cette proposition en derision sur les reseaux sociaux, estimant qu'un tel projet risquerait d'isoler davantage Israel de l'economie mondiale.

items.title: PCB releases Sufiyan Moqim from tri-series squad, adds Maaz Sadaqat as cover
items.description: The Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) on Sunday released left-arm wrist spinner Sufiyan Moqim from the national men’s squad for the ongoing One-day International tri-series involving England and Sri Lanka, citing the nature of the pitches in Lahore, while adding left-handed batter Maaz Sadaqat as cover for players carrying minor niggles. In a brief statement, the PCB said Sufiyan had been released from the squad “keeping in view the nature of Lahore pitches” and would return to domestic cricket. Maaz, meanwhile, had been added as cover for players with minor niggles. The move comes as the tri-series shifts to the Gaddafi Stadium after the opening three matches in Rawalpindi. Pakistan have won both their league games so far, beating Sri Lanka by 37 runs and England by 87, and face England again in Lahore on Sunday. The pitches in Rawalpindi generally favoured pace, limiting opportunities for specialist spinners. Sufiyan, who hails from Azad Kashmir, has represented Pakistan in limited-overs cricket since making his T20I debut in 2023. He is best known for his record-equalling figures of five for three against Zimbabwe in a T20 International and was named Player of the Tournament in the 2026 Pakistan Super League while playing for Peshawar Zalmi. In ODIs, he has taken eight wickets in four matches. Maaz, 21, has attracted attention with his aggressive batting. The Peshawar-born left-hander made an immediate impact on his ODI debut against Bangladesh earlier this year and recently impressed in the T20I series against Sri Lanka, scoring consecutive half-centuries, including a blistering 96 off 51 balls that helped Pakistan post their highest T20I total at home. An occasional left-arm orthodox spinner, Maaz had initially been left out of the tri-series squad. The updated squad, led by Shaheen Shah Afridi, now includes Maaz as Pakistan continue their campaign in Lahore ahead of the final on Oct 31 at the same venue.

items.title: 'Not a single tree' will be cut down to upgrade Islamabad's F-9 Park, interior minister assures residents
items.description: Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi on Sunday assured the residents of Islamabad that “not a single tree” will be cut down during the planned upgradation of the city’s F-9 Park. In a post on X, the minister shared an Instagram video of an Islamabad resident requesting that if the park were to be developed, more greenery be planted instead of concrete buildings. In his response, Naqvi recognised that F-9 Park — also known as Fatima Jinnah Park — “holds a special place in the hearts” of Islamabad residents and clarified that no trees would be removed in the process of developing the park. “Let me make it absolutely clear that not a single tree will be cut, 100 per cent guaranteed,” he said. He further vowed that there would be “no new concrete structures”. Instead, the planned upgrades included “better lighting, a beautiful lake, coffee shops, improved walkways” and the plantation of “thousands” of more trees in the park, the interior minister added. “Our only goal is to make F-9 Park greener, safer, more beautiful, and more enjoyable for families and visitors,” he said. Naqvi has previously shared plans to upgrade and improve recreational facilities around Islamabad, working with the Capital Development Authority (CDA) to create a “more developed, clean, green, beautiful, safe, environmentally sustainable and citizen-friendly capital” while enhancing its tourism potential. In April, he sought a comprehensive plan for transforming F-9 Park on the model of London’s Hyde Park, and for developing recreational facilities near Shahdara Dam. However, development projects in the historically green city have not always been favourably received by residents, inciting concerns particularly over deforestation and clearance of land for residential areas. At the start of this year, a large-scale tree removal drive took place in at least three locations in the Islamabad Capital Territory (ICT), including around the Shakarparian area, sparking widespread public criticism. The CDA maintained that only paper mulberry trees were removed as they had been causing pollen allergies , and Minister of State for Interior Tallal Chaudhry assured lawmakers that a greater number of trees would be planted in the coming months. In 2024, the Supreme Court (SC) took notice of the removal of trees in F-9 Park and restrained the CDA from cutting trees in the area. The CDA, in response, told the SC that about 7,000 paper mulberry trees had been cut down because they caused allergies.

items.title: Ghanaian fishermen recount how they survived on fresh fish when they got stranded at sea
items.description: A 29-year-old Ghanaian fisherman has recounted how he and six colleagues survived nearly two weeks at sea after their canoe’s outboard motor broke down, leaving them without adequate food and drinking water. Kwamena Nkum said the fishermen’s provisions ran out five days after the engine failure, forcing them to depend on fish they caught and eventually burn parts of their canoe to prepare meals. The seven men, all from Sekondi, embarked on a fishing expedition to Axim in the Western Region on October 9, 2026, aboard a canoe named Second Chance. Their journey took a dangerous turn three days later when the outboard motor stopped working. Efforts to repair the engine proved unsuccessful, leaving them stranded at sea. “We usually spend five days at sea, but this time, our motor became faulty on the third day. It just went off. We tried to fix it, but it didn’t work. Our food and water got finished,” Mr Nkum recounted. He said the fishermen resorted to drinking seawater after their supplies were exhausted, boiling it in an attempt to reduce its salt concentration. They initially ate fish from their catch, but some of the fish spoiled and had to be discarded. The men subsequently used hooks and lines to catch fresh fish for food. Mr Nkum said the fishermen had fuel and matches to make fire but eventually ran out of charcoal, compelling them to burn wood taken from their canoe to cook. After drifting for several days, the men eventually sighted land during the night. One fisherman who was still awake alerted the others. They switched on their mobile phones and later received a call from a friend, Kingsley, who was in contact with people back home. Mr Nkum said they contacted their fishing leaders and attempted to establish their location. Although they initially believed they were in Togo, they later discovered they had drifted into Beninese waters. “We had no food left. We were very hungry,” he said. According to him, Kingsley and the fishing leaders contacted the chief fisherman in Benin, who provided the stranded men with food and water. The fishermen subsequently received assistance from local fishing communities and the Beninese and Togolese navies. They were eventually handed over to the Ghana Navy by a Togolese naval vessel at the Ghana-Togo maritime border on October 21, 2026. The men later arrived safely at the Fishing Harbour in Tema following a joint search-and-rescue operation. The fishermen were identified as Kofi Emmanuel, 32; Uncle Amoah, 45; Kwamena Nkum, 29; Kofi Aboagye, 36; Doboa, 35; Agya Badu, 42; and Kwamena Akyem, 40. Reflecting on the ordeal, Mr Nkum said carrying a second outboard motor could have helped prevent the emergency from escalating, stressing the importance of having backup equipment for fishing expeditions.

items.title: Ça médit sur TikTok (le billet d’Omar DIOUF)
items.description: Diodio Glow Skin, Rox (encore elle), Adamo, Kaliphone… Une nouvelle affaire dakaroise sur TikTok. À la longue, on croirait que ce réseau social chinois est créé pour les potins sénégalais. En tout cas, c’est comme si. On y calomnie, insulte, règle des comptes à longueur d’heures, de journées, de mois… Certaines loueraient même les services d’énergumènes pour se charger du sale boulot, faire mal virtuellement à ses adversaires ou ennemies. Il y a trois jours, la dame Nogaye Kara écopait d’une amende financière pour discours contraire aux bonnes mœurs. Lors d’un live, elle se crêpait le chignon avec une certaine Mimi. À la longue, on se perd dans ce mélodrame à la Sénégalaise dans TikTok. À défaut de faire bon usage des technologies, certains de nos compatriotes en abusent en radotage de mensonges, en diffamation et autres commérages. La Division spéciale de cybersécurité et les procureurs ont vraiment du pain sur la planche… omar.diouf@lesoleil.sn

items.title: Art can give ecological restoration a local voice – World Resources Institute
items.description: The World Resources Institute (WRI) says art and culture can help make ecological restoration more meaningful to local communities. This is according to the institute’s Landscape Restoration Manager for the Ghana Cocoa Belt, Eric Lartey, who made this known at the inaugural Climate x Culture Summit in Accra on Thursday, October 22. “Restoration is more about people,” Mr Lartey said, explaining that music, oral traditions, festivals and customary practices shape how many Ghanaian communities relate to land, forests, water and biodiversity. He said integrating culture can connect restoration to community identity and make use of traditional ecological knowledge, which “can also inform more effective restoration practices.” Mr Lartey highlighted the Restoration Artists Network (RAN), a global initiative under the WRI that brings together musicians, visual artists, storytellers and cultural leaders to make ecological restoration more accessible. “Artists are powerful storytellers and cultural influencers,” he said, describing their ability to translate technical restoration concepts into simple, engaging messages. He cited a collaboration between Ghanaian and American artists that produced six songs drawing on Ghanaian musical traditions and local languages. The project aims to give landscape restoration “a local and a human voice,” he said. “Art is an access point. It can invite attention, stimulate conversation,” Mr Lartey said. He added that art can help people see themselves in a story that might otherwise feel technical or distant, while cautioning that it cannot replace investment, science or policy. @theculturejoint Okyeame Kwame at the Climate x Culture Summit 2026 which brought together voices from sustainability, the creative industries and culture to explore how we can make climate action more practical, inclusive and part of everyday life. Together, we can turn creativity into climate action. ♬ original sound – Culture Joint “If we want restoration effort to endure, it must be locally led and culturally grounded,” he said, pointing to Restore Local as a framework for the approach. The summit, themed “Designing Sustainable Creative Experiences For Africa,” was organised by Culture Joint Media in partnership with Ghana’s Minister of State for Climate Change & Sustainability at the Presidency. It brought together stakeholders from the climate, creative, business, media and technology sectors to explore how culture and creativity can contribute to climate action and sustainable development. items.title: Naufrage du Prospector 5 : Oligui Nguema promet de rendre publiques les conclusions de l’enquête
items.description: Mobiliser tous les moyens de l’État, informer les familles en priorité et faire la lumière sur le sinistre. Après le naufrage du Prospector 5 au large de Mayumba, Brice Clotaire Oligui Nguema annonce avoir donné des instructions au gouvernement. Il exige également une coopération totale de BW Energy, alors que cinq travailleurs restent portés disparus. « Les Gabonais ont le droit de savoir ce qui s’est passé » : Oligui Nguema face à l’exigence de vérité après le naufrage du Prospector 5. © D.R. «Les Gabonais ont le droit de savoir ce qui s’est passé.» Dans un message publié sur sa page Facebook, Brice Clotaire Oligui Nguema s’engage sur la transparence de l’enquête concernant le naufrage de la plateforme de forage Prospector 5, survenu samedi 24 octobre au large de Mayumba. Le chef de l’État affirme que les investigations établiront les causes et les responsabilités et que «ses conclusions seront rendues publiques» . Tous les moyens de l’État mobilisés Le président dit suivre «heure par heure» les opérations de recherche et de sauvetage des cinq travailleurs portés disparus. Il annonce avoir demandé au gouvernement de mobiliser tous les moyens de l’État, en premier lieu la Marine nationale, afin que les recherches se poursuivent « sans relâche » et que les familles soient informées en priorité. Brice Clotaire Oligui Nguema indique également s’être entretenu avec le directeur général de BW Energy. Selon son récit, celui-ci lui a assuré que les équipes de l’entreprise interviennent avec Borr Drilling et les autorités gabonaises pour retrouver les disparus. «Je lui ai rappelé que l’État attend de l’opérateur une coopération totale, sur les recherches comme sur l’enquête» , souligne le chef de l’État. Une exigence de sécurité pour les travailleurs en mer Le président adresse ses pensées aux disparus et à leurs proches, tout en saluant les 110 personnes sauvées et le courage des secours intervenus dans la nuit. Il exprime aux familles «la solidarité entière de la Nation» . Au-delà de l’urgence, il affirme vouloir porter une exigence de sécurité auprès de chaque opérateur présent dans les eaux gabonaises : «Ceux qui travaillent en mer pour notre pays doivent pouvoir le faire en sécurité.» L’article Naufrage du Prospector 5 : Oligui Nguema promet de rendre publiques les conclusions de l’enquête est apparu en premier sur Gabonreview.com | Actualité du Gabon | .
